Have a look at my answer to a similar question:

What should a mechanical engineer study to move into audio signal processing?

As for UK universities that do acoustics:

Southampton has the largest acoustics lab in the world, working mainly on noise and vibration, railway and aircraft acoustics, underwater acoustics, 3D audio and more.

Salford isn’t a famous university, but it is very strong in acoustics: building acoustics, psychoacoustics and so on. By the way, Trevor Cox, one of the professors there, writes a really good blog.

Others include York, mainly virtual acoustics, and UCL, where Professor Jian Kang works on soundscape.

Elsewhere in Europe:

RWTH Aachen University: virtual, building and medical acoustics. It started on virtual acoustics very early and ranks among the best in the world. Vorländer’s Auralization is the definitive work in the field.

Aalto University, Finland: virtual acoustics and speech signal processing.

KU Leuven, Belgium: possibly the second-largest acoustics lab after Southampton. Noise and vibration, numerical simulation, and a lot of acoustic metamaterials lately.

Chalmers, Sweden: the head of the group, Wolfgang, made his name on tire noise; now several young professors work on virtual acoustics and spatial audio.

The acoustics institute in Le Mans, France: also enormous, and lately thriving on acoustic metamaterials.

Several other German universities are strong too: TU Berlin, TUM, Oldenburg and others.

The Swiss research institute Empa also does excellent acoustics, with real strength in virtual, environmental and materials acoustics.

Typing on my phone is a pain and I have work tomorrow, so I’ll stop here. I’ll come back and go into more detail when I have time.

For more on acoustics (popular science, curiosities, little-known facts, industrial applications and where the field is heading), see my Zhihu column Acoustics: Tech You Can Hear and my WeChat Official Account, Ziyu Acoustics.
